full_judgment:
Fazle Munim CJ: This appeal arises from the Judgment and order in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1984 and suo motu Rule No.41 of 1984 passed by a Bench of the High Court Division, Rangpur (Mr. justice Mustafa Kamal and Mr. Justice Muhammad Abdul Wahab) on 28th November 1984, convicting the appellant for contempt of Court and sentencing him to suffer simple imprisonment for 7 days and to pay a fine of Taka 1000 and in default, simple imprisonment for 3 days more. 

 2. Facts as stated in the complaint against the appellant by respondent No. 2 who is Munsif-Magistrate, Chilmari are that while he was conducting criminal cases in Court on 6th December 1983, appellant who is an Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Chilmari, Upazila, Kurigram sat by his side and said that respondent No. 2 should take practical training from him as to how cases are filed, how depositions are taken, under what sections depositions are recorded, etc. these utterances were made in the presence of Advocates, Court Sub-Inspector and the litigant public who were inside the Court room. 

 3. On 26th December 1983 appellant summoned respondent No. 2 in his chapter and in presence of one of the parties to a Criminal proceeding and directed respondent No. 2 to dispose of the case according to his instructions and advice. On 22nd December 1983 the appellant instructed the Bench Officer of the Criminal Court and others not to work in the Court of respondent No. 2. 

 4. Also, the appellant interfered with the leave and annual vacation of respondent No. 2. Respondent No. 2 wrote a letter to District and Sessions Judge, Rangpur regarding their matters. This led to all kinds of pressure upon him by the appellant. On 24th January 1984, District and Sessions Judge, Rangpur forwarded the complaint to Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh for placing the matter before a Bench of the High Court Division, Rangpur. The Bench at Rangpur, after hearing the respondent by order dated 19th March 1984, issued Rule upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be convicted for contempt of Court being Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1984. 

 5. During the pendency of the above Rule for contempt District and Sessions Judge, Rangpur forwarded two representations made by respondent No. 2 to the Government praying for his transfer from Chilmari. On perusal of the representations the learned Judges of the High Court Division issued a Suo Motu of contempt on the appellant to show cause why he should not be punished for repeating the offence of contempt of Court, the Rule being numbered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 1984. 

 7. After perusal of the affidavits and hearing of the parties the learned Judges of the High Court Division discharged the Rule in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 1984 but found the appellant guilty of gross contempt of Court in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 1984 and sentenced him to suffer simple imprisonment for 7 days and to fine of Taka 1,000 only in default, to suffer simple imprisonment for a further period of 3 days. Being aggrieved the appellant filed the aforesaid appeal before this Court. 

 8. Mr. SR Pal, Counsel for the appellant, attempted to show that the appellant did not commit contempt of Court. It appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division have elaborately considered the facts and circumstances of the case, which appeared from the exhaustive affidavits, submitted by the appellant and respondent No. 2 appellant's Counsel submitted that the lack of evidence in his case led to miscarriage of justice. It seems that he was not satisfied with affidavit evidence, which was fully considered by the learned Judges of the High Court Division in reaching conclusions on whether contempt was committed by the appellant. 

 "The question of examining witnesses does not arise at all. The witnesses that the contemner wants to examine are very much under his thumb. They are his direct subordinates or persons on whom he yields immense influence by virtue of his continuing position as the chief executive of the Upazila. We do not think that in the facts and circumstances of this case examination of witnesses is as all warranted. On the face of it the contemner has put up a false and fabricated defence. 

 "The incident of sitting by the side of the Munsif-Magistrate and telling him in presence of Advocates and litigants as to how to conduct a criminal case is an unprecedented and unwarranted interference with the administration of justice. It is deliberately calculated to lower the image of judiciary in public eyes. It is a contumacious disregard of the dignity of a Court of law, which must be visited with appropriate punishment. We find the contemner guilty of contempt of Court on this allegation." 

 14. Though a little unusual, the judgment of the High Court Division has been extensively quoted above, this has been so because, appellant's Counsel, instead of advancing lengthy submissions, briefly mentioned the background of the case and took time. Adjournment of the appeal was grant for a day. Next day, an application tendering unqualified apology was filed on behalf of the appellant where, in one paragraph, it was stated as follows: 

 16. Mr AW Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, referred to a few decisions on the point which, in order to give as well as derive true insight into the problem arising out of contempt of Court, need consideration. In the case of Yusuf Ali Khan vs The State, PLD 1970 SC 350, the Pakistan Supreme Court in dealing with the question of acceptance of apology observed that "an apology in contempt cases can be mitigating circumstance only if the contemner surrenders himself unconditionally to the judgment of the Court.:" 

 18. Reference was made to an earlier case decided by itself where the Court had observed that "in considering whether the apology should be accepted or not, a few facts should be taken into consideration." These facts, as mentioned by the Court, are: 

 "(i) 	As to whether the appellant appreciated that his act was within the mischief of contempt; 

 19. In the case of Asharam M. Jain vs AT Gupta, AIR 1983 SC 1151 the Indian Supreme Court has, while, considering whether unqualified apology tendered by the contemner should be accepted or not, referred to a few principles for guidance of the Court. While it is necessary to remember that in dealing with a contemner, the Judges should not be hypersensitive where distortions and criticisms overstep the limits, it is at the same time equally important to deflate vulgar denunciation by dignified bearing condescending indifference and repudiation by judicial rectitude. In stating the predicament in which the Judges function and conduct themselves in discharging the high duties of office, the Court observed: 

 21. In the case of LD Jaikioal vs State of UP AIR 1984 SC 1374, the Indian Supreme Court observed that "this was a 'paper' apology and the expression of sorrow came from the pen, not from his heart. For it is one thing to 'say' sorry-it is another to 'feel' sorry". The learned Judge who delivered the judgment observed that the Court "cannot subscribe to the slap-say sorry and forget" school of thought in administration of contempt jurisprudence". 

 23. In the present case the appellant committed contempt of Court by his several acts referred to in the judgment of the High Court Division. He ought to have thrown himself at the mercy of the Court as soon as the Rule for contempt was served upon him. But, without doing so, he preferred to file affidavit after affidavit in justification of those acts or explaining them away. Even when he was convicted for contempt of Court and sentenced as above, he proceeded in the appeal before us, to show that the judgment of the High Court Division and the findings arrived at by the learned Judges were wrong. It is only when this Court expressed itself in no uncertain terms in showing disapproval of his conduct that the aforesaid application tendering apology was filed. In view of the circumstance as mentioned above, we find ourselves unable to condone his action which is not only humiliating to the presiding officer of a Court, however small it may be, it also amounts to clear defiance of the majesty of law.
